question: For a symmetrical distribution, we have:
solution:
The correct answer is** mean = median = mode.**

** [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__**

__
 
• **For a symmetrical distribution, we have: mean = median = mode:**

 
 
• In a symmetrical distribution, the left and right sides of the distribution are mirror images of each other.
 
• This symmetry implies that the central tendency measures (mean, median, and mode) are all located at the center of the distribution and are equal.
 
• In financial enterprises, such distributions often simplify the analysis of data, as the central point provides a clear and unambiguous measure of central tendency.
 
• For example, if analyzing the returns of a well-diversified portfolio that follows a normal distribution, the mean, median, and mode of the returns will be the same, providing a clear indication of the expected return.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **mean > median > mode:**

 
 
• This relationship typically occurs in a positively skewed distribution, where the tail on the right side is longer than on the left.
 
• In financial enterprises, this may be observed in income distributions where a small number of high-income individuals skew the mean upwards.
 
 
 
• **mean 
 
• This relationship is seen in a negatively skewed distribution, where the tail on the left side is longer than on the right.
 
• In finance, this could be seen in the distribution of losses where a few large losses pull the mean down below the median and mode.
 
 
 
• **mean 
 
• This scenario is uncommon and does not typically represent any standard distribution pattern.
 
• It could theoretically occur in some specific, non-standard distributions but is not generally applicable in typical financial data analysis.
